A1.justification: Both PDFs describe NLPrompt and provide readable main text, figures, tables, equations, and Appendices A–E. The complete materials support reliable matching despite expanded experiments and relocated content.

before.justification: v1 reports original noisy-label classification experiments, purification comparisons, few-shot analyses, and component ablations, including SUN397 results in Appendix C.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds experiments on other prompting methods, hyperparameter sensitivity, alternative noise allocation, Mixup, and computational cost.

M1.justification: Section 5 and Algorithm 1 retain text-feature OT prototypes, pseudo-label-based partitioning, CE for the clean subset, and MAE for the noisy subset. Applying NLPrompt to other prompting methods adds evaluations without documenting a changed NLPrompt procedure.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same eight synthetic-noise datasets, including SUN397 in the appendix, and Food101N. The additions use retained classification coverage; model variants, noise-allocation controls, and computational scaling concern experimental settings rather than new datasets or tasks.

E2.justification: v2 substantially expands evaluated comparators: Table 3 compares VPT, MaPLe, and PromptSRC with their NLPrompt-enhanced counterparts, and Table A10 adds CoOp+Mixup. Existing CoOp, GCE, JoAPR, and purification comparators remain; the purification comparison moves to Table A7.

E3.justification: Added protocols test other prompting configurations, context lengths of 1–32, OT regularization coefficients from 10^-4 to 1, classwise noise allocation on DTD, and computational scaling. Table 4 adds a 10% noise condition. The original default training settings remain stated; the new explanation of global noise allocation does not establish that those experiments changed.

E4.justification: v2 adds substantial analyses of transfer across prompting methods, context-length and OT-regularization sensitivity, robustness to noise-allocation procedure, and computational overhead. It also extends the component ablation to lower noise. The original purification analysis is retained in Appendix C.2, not newly introduced.

E5.justification: Both versions specify averages over three runs with different seeds. v2 additionally reports numerical ± quantities in the context-length ablation, Table A8, without defining whether they represent standard deviations or another uncertainty measure. No increase in run count is stated.

E6.justification: Most JoAPR values in Table 1 are revised, changing some rankings: at 75% asymmetric noise on Caltech101, its reported accuracy changes from 45.83 to 81.90, exceeding the unchanged NLPrompt value of 81.07. Several NLPrompt values also change, including OxfordPets at 50% symmetric noise, 83.17 to 84.87, and the Flowers102 ablation at 50%, 91.21 to 92.30. New results appear in Table 3, Tables A8–A10, Figure A4, and the timing analysis. Table 4 adds 10% noise results and averages over four conditions instead of three.

T1.justification: The feature decomposition, assumptions, Theorem 4.2, and Appendix E derivations and proofs are mathematically unchanged after matching equation renumbering. v2 adds a proof outline and intuitive explanations, without new formal results or corrections.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction contributions, and conclusion retain the same claims about PromptMAE robustness, its feature-learning explanation, PromptOT purification, and NLPrompt effectiveness. Additional experiments do not redefine these core claims.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations concerning transferability, hyperparameter robustness, small OT overhead, and why global noise allocation can be harder than classwise allocation. Appendix E adds intuition and a rationale for interpreting experiments through binary-classification theory. The existing low-noise limitation and imbalance-related future work remain.

D1.justification: v2 clarifies dataset-wide noise allocation versus JoAPR's classwise allocation and documents OT matching dimensions and timings, including 0.00173 seconds per epoch versus 4.352 seconds for backpropagation on Caltech101. The code link, hardware, optimizer, and default training disclosures are retained.

R1.justification: v2 adds references for VPT, PromptSRC, and several feature-learning studies, modestly broadening the context. MaPLe was already cited in v1. The main related-work narrative and novelty positioning remain substantially unchanged; venue updates and duplicate-reference changes do not introduce distinct research.

P1.justification: Most prose and the overall section sequence remain intact. The purification discussion moves from Section 6.5 to Appendix C.2, Section 6.5 now covers generalization, and Appendix C gains subsections. Appendix E adds an outline and intuition and relocates existing explanatory prose; terminology corrections and acknowledgements are also added.

P2.justification: v2 substantially expands and rearranges experimental displays through a new generalization table, Tables A8–A10, and Figure A4. It relocates the purification table to A7, expands Table 4 with a 10% column, reorders Table 1's dataset blocks, and reduces Figure 3's displayed size. Existing main-figure content is retained apart from a label correction.

improvement.justification: The added transfer, sensitivity, matched-noise, and timing evaluations address practical questions left untested in v1 and strengthen assessment of NLPrompt's applicability. The gain is limited by reporting inconsistencies: Section 6.4 still claims consistent high-noise superiority, although revised Table 1 shows JoAPR ahead at 75% asymmetric noise on Caltech101 and 75% symmetric noise on OxfordPets. Overall, the additional evidence provides a useful but qualified improvement.
